doc.title: Bobby Johnson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Southern college bands and the book he would write
summary: Southern college bands produced fine musicians, many of whom went to New York; he wants to write a book about them.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: bands. The Alabama State Teacher’s College at Montgomery, the Tennessee State at Nashville, and then several other colleges, they’ve always had great bands and great musicians turn out, like Dwike Mitchell and all those guys from Jacksonville, Edward Waters College. But maybe that is because of the fact that there’s not that much work, you know, when you come out of school. If I told you when I was like maybe, before I came up here, I was offered about maybe ten scholarships, not anything other than playing the trumpet. And at Alabama State, that was a state college, run by state money, tax money. We had to make our own breakfast, you understand? I didn’t attend very long because there was always something better than that. But I’m writing a book, I’d like to write a book about the southern colleges, southern bands that didn’t really make it. Because in New York, if you came to New York you were a New York musician. That’s the reason why I came. But bands like Don Albert, Johnson’s Happy Pals from Richmond Virginia, and most all of those musicians came to New York and got with big bands you know? And that’s just about it. One of these days I’ll write the book, maybe you’ll finish it for me.
